Since $G\ge0$, its integral on every compact $K$ is zero. The compact
intervals $[0,T]$ exhaust $[0,1)$, so $G=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.
If a support point $s$ had $G(s)>0$, continuity would give a relative
neighbourhood on which $G$ stays positive. After restricting to a compact
interval containing that neighbourhood, the defining property of support
would give it positive $\mu$-mass, contradicting the zero integral.
Therefore
$$
G(s)=0\qquad(s\in S).
$$

statements.markdown:
There is also a global alternative to compact mass removal. Atom addition
still gives $G\ge0$. Now replace $\mu$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\mu$,
or equivalently $\gamma$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$, for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. This preserves admissibility, and its direction
$-\gamma$ lies in $L^1$, although it may be unbounded. The first
variation in §3.2 therefore applies. The signed interchange is justified by
$$
\int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds)
 =\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
 \le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$
Consequently
$$
0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
 =-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds).
$$
Together with $G\ge0$, this gives $\int G\,d\mu=0$. Continuity
then gives $G=0$ on relative support, including zero, as in §3.3.
Finite weighted mass is sufficient throughout, with no assumption of
finite total mass or of a density for $\mu$.
statements.note: Lean uses only compact removal; this global scaling proof is not formalised. The steps it shares with compact removal are in the Lean.
